The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".

Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.
Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued.
Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."

evidenceRecords.text: ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot has arrived back in Europe, landing in Cologne, Germany, following her return to Earth with Crew-12 after 237 days, nearly eight months, aboard the International Space Station for her εpsilon mission.
On 9 October Sophie boarded a French Air and Space Force Airbus A330 MRTT Phénix bound for ESA’s European Astronaut Centre (EAC) in Cologne, Germany.
She landed at 04:21 GMT / 06:21 CEST on 10 October and was warmly welcomed on the apron by family, friends, colleagues, journalists and representatives from ESA Member States.
“We are delighted to welcome back our ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot who embodied our values through her successful mission,” says Josef Aschbacher, ESA’s Director General.
Sophie spent a total of 237 days, 5 hours and 18 minutes in space after being launched on 13 February 2026 from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, USA.
The εpsilon mission set a new European record for the longest single spaceflight, exceeding by more than 35 days the previous record held by ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano for his Beyond mission.
Crew-12 is also the longest SpaceX Dragon mission to date, surpassing the previous record of 235 days set by Crew-8.
Sophie is the second European woman, after ESA astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti, and the first French woman to conduct an Extra Vehicular Activity (EVA), or spacewalk.
Sophie completed three spacewalks in 14 days, spending a total of 19 hours and 42 minutes working outside the Station.

Throughout εpsilon, Sophie carried out a wide range of European experiments spanning fields from health research to materials science, biology, fluid physics, radiation physics and fundamental science.

Over the course of Expedition 74 and 75, Sophie worked on experiments and payloads for International Space Station partners, contributing to the international research programme carried out aboard the orbiting laboratory.
Sophie also spent around 218 hours working on 35 European payloads, and about 25 hours on ESA systems maintenance or upgrades in Columbus, Europe’s microgravity research facility in orbit.
Her return now marks the successful completion of an outstanding mission aboard the International Space Station, says Daniel Neuenschwander, ESA Director of Human and Robotic Exploration.

evidenceRecords.text: When police need to launch a drone during an emergency, every minute counts.
But when that mission involves controlled airspace near an airport, getting the necessary FAA authorization can add another step before the drone takes off.
Versaterm wants to make that process simpler.

The public safety technology company has integrated Versaterm Aloft’s FAA airspace authorization capabilities directly into Versaterm DroneSense, allowing public safety agencies to request and receive Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) approvals without switching applications or coordinating manually with the FAA.
The idea is straightforward: bring airspace authorization into the same workflow agencies already use to dispatch and manage their drones.
For Drone as First Responder (DFR) programs, that could mean less time spent navigating separate systems and more time getting eyes on an unfolding situation.
LAANC provides a streamlined way for drone operators to obtain FAA authorization to fly in controlled airspace at approved altitudes.
It’s particularly relevant to public safety agencies operating near airports, where authorization requirements can affect how quickly a drone can launch.
With the new integration, agencies can request authorizations directly within DroneSense.
The connected workflow brings computer-aided dispatch (CAD), drone operations and FAA airspace compliance together, with near-real-time authorization processing and automatic compliance reporting.
That could be useful during time-sensitive missions such as search and rescue operations and tactical responses, where dispatchers and pilots need to coordinate quickly.

“Readiness shouldn’t depend on how many systems a pilot can juggle under pressure,” says Versaterm CEO Steve Seoane, explaining that authorization should become part of launching a drone rather than another task pilots must complete beforehand.

She had also earlier worked as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs at the Department of Homeland Security.
Zacharia, in a post on X, thanked Trump and said "his leadership is a blessing to this country."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our country and communicating to the American people the major wins that the administration is making every single day," Zacharia said. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out."
Zacharia said her predecessor Leavitt was "fabulous" and that she set a "high standard" to meet for the press secretary job.
Trump had announced that Leavitt would resign in August to spend more time with her young children and family.
Leavitt took a combative approach to questions from the White House press corps during her tenure as press secretary.

In January, she called a White House reporter a "left-wing hack" after a question regarding the fatal US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shooting of American citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis.
She also had to defend Trump's controversial handling of the Epstein files and the ongoing Iran war.
Leavitt managed to stay in the role for over 18 months — a long tenure for a high-stress job under a demanding president.

evidenceRecords.text: Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal.

As first reported in MacRumors, Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.”

Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.”)
In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook).

But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down, with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data.
“The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said.
It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.”
On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal.
The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted.
Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans.

Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own, so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app.
Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree.
